q.intro.text: A dab of wet paint sits at P on a sheet of graph paper. You fold the sheet along the crease m, and press it flat.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one. The picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s0.text: The fold moves P straight toward the crease, at a right angle to m. It meets m at the point M.

e.s1.text: From P to M: two diagonal steps, grid corner to grid corner.

e.s2.text: Two more steps beyond m. That is P prime. P prime is as far behind m as P is in front of it.

e.s3.text: Fold along m, and P lands exactly on P prime. The paint prints at spot two.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why does the paint print at spot two, and not straight across the page at spot one?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. Folding along m moves P at a right angle to m, so P prime is on the perpendicular from P.

e.w-across.text: Only when m runs straight up and down the page. Here m is slanted, so the right angle is with m, not with the page.

e.w-far.text: Spots one and three are just as far from m as P. Only spot two is also on the perpendicular from P.

t.intro.text: Now reflect triangle A B C in m, one vertex at a time. Vertex A is done for you.

t.a.text: A is two diagonal steps from m, so A prime is two steps beyond it.

t.count.text: Your turn. Count the diagonal steps from B to m, at a right angle to m.

t.c-ok.text: Yes. Three steps from B to m.

t.c-across.text: That counts squares straight across the page. Step diagonally, corner to corner, at a right angle to m.

t.c-points.text: Count the steps, not the corners. Start counting after B.

t.c-other.text: Step from B toward m along the other diagonal, and count the steps.

t.spot.text: Now count three steps beyond m. Which spot is B prime?

t.s-ok.text: Yes. Three steps beyond m. That's B prime.

t.s-short.text: That spot is only two steps beyond m. Count three, the same as from B to m.

t.s-long.text: That spot is four steps beyond m. One too many. Count three, the same as from B to m.

t.c.text: C is on m. Where is C prime?

t.cc-ok.text: Right. C is zero steps from m, so C prime is zero steps beyond. C prime is C.

t.cc-no.text: C is on m: zero steps from it. Zero steps beyond m is still C. Points on the line stay put.

t.join.text: Join A prime, B prime and C prime, in order. Going A, B, C turns clockwise. Which way does A prime, B prime, C prime turn?

t.o-ok.text: Right. The order is reversed. A reflection flips the triangle over. A slide never would.

t.o-no.text: Trace it again. A prime, B prime, C prime goes the other way round. A reflection always reverses the order.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked spot two, and you were right. Now you can say why: at a right angle to m, just as far beyond.

t.cb-across.text: At the start you picked spot one, straight across the page. The fold moves P at a right angle to m, so the paint printed at spot two.

t.cb-far.text: At the start you picked spot three. It is as far from m as P, but moved along m. The image is on the perpendicular: spot two.

p.intro.text: Riley says: Q is the image of P in m, because Q is on the other side of m, and just as far from it.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.k1.text: The image of P has to be on the perpendicular from P to m,

p.k2.text: But Q is not on that perpendicular,

p.k3.text: So Q is not the image of P. The image, P prime, is two steps beyond M,

p.c1.text: Right. A fold moves every point at a right angle to the crease.

p.c2.text: And P Q crosses m on a slant. Q is moved along m, away from the perpendicular.

p.c3.text: P is two steps from m, so P prime is two steps beyond M, on the same perpendicular. Q is not P prime.

p.x-far.text: That is Riley's mistake. Equal distance is not enough. Q must also be on the perpendicular from P.

p.x-side.text: The other side is not enough. The image has to be at a right angle to m, and just as far.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That's a proof. Three claims, each with its reason, and the picture backs every one. Same distance is not enough. The right angle matters too.
